sections.html:
Madison County is in east central Indiana, and its seat is Anderson. The 2020 census counted 130,129 people in the county and 54,788 in Anderson. Besides Anderson, the county has the city of Alexandria and part of Elwood, plus smaller communities such as Ovid and Edgewood Village. The land is nearly flat, with some hills along the White River and Fall Creek.

The median home here is worth $147,700 and was built in 1965. That is an older housing stock, which is worth knowing whether you are arguing about an assessment or trying to sell a house that needs a new roof, furnace or plumbing.

sections.h2: Who handles Madison County property tax
sections.html:
Property tax runs through three offices in Anderson, and each one answers a different question. The Auditor and Treasurer share the Madison County Government Center at 16 East 9th Street, Anderson, IN 46016. Calling the wrong office wastes a trip, so match your question to the table first.

OfficeWhat it handlesWhere to reach it
AssessorAssessed values and Form 130 appealsAnderson
AuditorDeductions, deed transfers, redemption after a tax saleGovernment Center; (765) 641-9422 or (765) 641-9505
TreasurerCollects payments, online payment, tax sale paymentsGovernment Center, 16 East 9th Street

Hours and holiday closures are posted on the county's contact page. If a question about your value lands at the Treasurer's desk, expect to be sent on to the Assessor.

The Auditor handles the homestead deduction, the over 65 deduction, the blind or disabled deduction and the veteran deduction. You can file online, and the online form asks for your parcel number. Add an email address before you submit so the office can reach you.

Have these ready before you start:

  • Your parcel number, which is printed on the tax bill.
  • An Indiana driver's license.
  • The last five digits of the Social Security number for you and your spouse.
  • For the over 65 deduction, an income tax return or a Social Security 1099.

Sellers should know that a deduction belongs to the person who files for it. A buyer applies for their own after closing, so the bill you paid with a homestead deduction may be higher for the next owner. Ask the Auditor what happens to a deduction on your parcel when the deed transfers.

The spring bill is due May 10 and the fall bill November 10, both paid to the county Treasurer. If either date lands on a weekend or holiday, you get the next business day. The county's tax system takes online payments, which is the quickest way to get a receipt.

Miss a due date and the Treasurer adds a 5 percent penalty, as long as you catch up inside 30 days and the parcel carries no older balance. Wait past that window, or have back taxes already, and the penalty doubles to 10 percent.

Falling further behind brings the tax sale. A property is eligible when it is delinquent for three or more installments, and the county posts its sale listings online through SRI Services. Once a parcel is certified for the sale, it cannot be paid online. The Treasurer takes those payments in person by cashier's check, money order or cash.

If a property has already been sold at a tax sale or a commissioners' sale, redemption goes through the Auditor's Office, not the Treasurer. Check the Auditor's tax sale list before you plan a closing, since it tells you whether your parcel is close to certification.

If your value looks too high, put your case on paper. Form 130 is filed with the county assessing official and ends up in front of the Property Tax Assessment Board of Appeals. June 15 is the deadline, and the year it counts toward depends on the date the county mailed your notice.

The process runs in steps:

  1. An informal meeting with the assessing official.
  2. A hearing before the board within 180 days of filing, with notice at least 30 days ahead.
  3. An appeal to the Indiana Board of Tax Review on Form 131 if you disagree, or if the board does not decide within 180 days.

An appraisal is optional. Recent sales of comparable homes are the best evidence you can bring, and with a county median of $147,700, a sale price near that range is a reasonable reference point if you think your value is too high.

Nobody is penalized for paying on last year's assessed value while an appeal is open. Lose the appeal and the difference comes due, so set that money aside.

sections.h2: What to settle with the county before closing
sections.html:
A handful of phone calls keeps a closing on schedule. Start with the Treasurer: confirm which installments are paid and whether anything is open. Then call the Auditor to ask whether the deductions on your parcel end with the sale and whether the parcel appears on the tax sale list. Last, if you have an appeal pending, tell the Assessor you are selling, since the outcome affects the bill that follows the house.

Bring the parcel number to every call. It identifies the property faster than the street address and keeps the three offices looking at the same record. If you inherited the house, also have the paperwork showing who may sign, because the title company will ask for it before it schedules a closing.

At the closing table the title company divides the year's tax between you and the buyer and pays off any open balance from your proceeds. Ask for the figures a few days ahead so you can compare them with the Treasurer's numbers and spot a mismatch while there is still time to fix it.

Madison County owners who sell as-is usually point to the age of the house and the repairs it needs: roof, plumbing and furnace costs, inherited homes, tenant problems and repair bills that exceed what the house would bring after fixing. If back taxes are part of the picture, a cash sale lets the title company pay the delinquent amount from the proceeds at closing.

The White River crosses the northern part of Anderson and Fall Creek runs through the south of the county. If a house sits near either one, ask for the flood zone on the survey or the lender's determination so nothing surprises a buyer later.

Before you accept an offer, gather the latest tax bill, the parcel number, proof that your installments are paid, and the paperwork for any open appeal. Tell the title company about all of it. A buyer who pays cash skips the lender's appraisal and repair demands, which is where sales on older houses tend to stall, but the title still has to be clean and the taxes settled.

When you want to compare routes, ask for a written cash offer and set it beside what listing would net after repairs, showings and carrying costs. You can then decide with real numbers in front of you.

faqs.q: When is Madison County property tax due?
faqs.a: Installments are due May 10 and November 10, and a weekend or holiday moves the date to the next business day. Payment goes to the county Treasurer.

faqs.q: Where is the Madison County Treasurer?
faqs.a: The Treasurer is in the Madison County Government Center, 16 East 9th Street, Anderson, IN 46016. Hours and holiday closures are on the county's contact page.

faqs.q: Can I pay Madison County taxes online?
faqs.a: Yes, the Treasurer takes online payments. A parcel certified for tax sale cannot be paid online and needs a cashier's check, money order or cash in person.

faqs.q: Who handles homestead deductions in Madison County?
faqs.a: The Auditor's Office. You need your parcel number, an Indiana driver's license and, for most filers, the last five digits of the Social Security number for you and your spouse.

faqs.q: What makes a Madison County property eligible for the tax sale?
faqs.a: A property is eligible when it is delinquent for three or more installments. The sale listings run online through SRI Services, and redemption goes through the Auditor.
